newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary new industry heads less political-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Hungary new industry heads less political-analysts.

text.p: Prime Minister Gyula Horn's nominations to replace industry and trade minister and other officials at the heart of Hungary's privatisation scandal appear to go some way towards taking politics out of the country's industrial policy, analysts said on Monday.

Horn last week appointed Judit Csiha as minister in charge of the state privatisation agency APV and Szabolcs Fazakas as minister of industry and trade to replace Tamas Suchman who will relinquish both portfolios on Tuesday.

Suchman, a close Horn ally, was sacked a week ago following a scandal involving the irregular payment of 804 million forints ($5.2 million) in fees to consultant Marta Tocsik for negotiating payments to municipalities for land used by state-owned companies.
The entire executive board of the state privatisation agency APV was also dismissed.

"The prime minister is saying he wants to see professionally well-trained and politically neutral people in these positions," said Istvan Stumpf, head of political sciences at the Hungarian Academy of Sciences.

Fazakas has spent most of his professional life in foreign trade. He was state secretary at the industry and trade ministry until this summer, when he was appointed ambassador to Bonn to promote further trade links with Germany, Hungary's biggest trading partner.

"Fazakas, because of his experience as ambassador in Germany and his contacts built up over the years with other Western investors will make foreign investors feel more comfortable than with Suchman," said political analyst Attila Ledenyi.

Stumpf said Csiha may seem a more political appointment in that she was once head of the Socialist Party faction in Budapest City Council but will be seen by most observers as an independent professional.
"Csiha is not part of any lobby group around APV. She has experience in privatisation affairs and as a lawyer has the professional competence for the job," he said.
Ledenyi agrees that Csiha is less of a political animal than Suchman was but believes that the Socialists' liberal coalition allies the Free Democrats will still have reservations about her.

"Csiha is a little more complicated (than Fazakas). She has a more political past and is less of a technocrat," he said, adding that the Free Democrats were looking for someone who could guarantee that privatisation is less politicised.
"They have not come up with any name of their own," he said. "They will probably live with her as she does have some relevant experience."
Horn also nominated head of the State Audit Office Arpad Kovacs as new APV board chairman and Andras Laszlo as general manager to replace Imre Szokai and Istvan Kocsis respectively.
Stumpf said the two APV nominations both have the respect of the business and legal community.

"Kovacs, as director of the State Audit Office, has a very good professional reputation among lawyers and public administrators and Laszlo has been a key person inside the industry and trade ministry on privatisation matters," he said.
"This is a very good message for all players in Hungary's privatisation process."
He added that the scandal will make no difference to the general thrust of privatisation.

"This is not a real privatisation scandal, it is about how money is distributed," Stumpf said. "There will be no change in prvatisation policy, except they will be more open and will give much more equal opportunity to those wishing to invest in Hungary."
